title: 15  Measures of spatial autocorrelation
text:
Exercise 15.2
First, create an uncorrelated variable, and confirm that it is uncorrelated:


R
Python




set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(nrow(grd))
moran.test(x, nb2listw(queen, style="W"), randomisation=FALSE, alternative="two.sided")
# 
#   Moran I test under normality
# 
# data:  x  
# weights: nb2listw(queen, style = "W")    
# 
# Moran I statistic standard deviate = 0.27024, p-value =
# 0.787
# alternative hypothesis: two.sided
# sample estimates:
# Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
#       0.002292497      -0.015873016       0.004518556




def moran_test(x, B):
    """Moran's I test under normality, two-sided, row-standardized weights"""
    W = B / B.sum(1, keepdims=True); n = len(x)
    S0 = W.sum(); S1 = 0.5 * ((W + W.T) ** 2).sum(); S2 = ((W.sum(1) + W.sum(0)) ** 2).sum()
    z = x - x.mean(); I = n / S0 * (z @ W @ z) / (z @ z)
    E = -1 / (n - 1)
    V = (n * n * S1 - n * S2 + 3 * S0 ** 2) / (S0 ** 2 * (n * n - 1)) - E ** 2
    Z = (I - E) / np.sqrt(V)
    return pd.Series(dict(I=I, expectation=E, variance=V, z=Z, p_value=2 * norm.sf(abs(Z))))

# the random numbers of the R solution (set.seed(1); rnorm(64)), as numpy cannot reproduce R's generator
xd = pd.read_csv("data/ch15_x.csv")
x, Var1 = xd.x.to_numpy(), xd.Var1.to_numpy().astype(float)
moran_test(x, B_queen)
# I              0.002292
# expectation   -0.015873
# variance       0.004519
# z              0.270239
# p_value        0.786976
# dtype: float64




Next inject patterning into the variable by adding a linear trend:


R
Python




x_t <- x + (0.15 * xy$Var1)
moran.test(x_t, nb2listw(queen, style="W"), randomisation=FALSE, alternative="two.sided")
# 
#   Moran I test under normality
# 
# data:  x_t  
# weights: nb2listw(queen, style = "W")    
# 
# Moran I statistic standard deviate = 3.0064, p-value =
# 0.002644
# alternative hypothesis: two.sided
# sample estimates:
# Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
#       0.186218071      -0.015873016       0.004518556




x_t = x + 0.15 * Var1
moran_test(x_t, B_queen)
# I              0.186218
# expectation   -0.015873
# variance       0.004519
# z              3.006404
# p_value        0.002644
# dtype: float64




Test again having taken the residuals from a linear model removing the injected trend:


R
Python




lm.morantest(lm(x_t ~ xy$Var1), nb2listw(queen, style="W"), alternative="two.sided")
# 
#   Global Moran I for regression residuals
# 
# data:  
# model: lm(formula = x_t ~ xy$Var1)
# weights: nb2listw(queen, style = "W")
# 
# Moran I statistic standard deviate = 0.28036, p-value =
# 0.7792
# alternative hypothesis: two.sided
# sample estimates:
# Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
#     -0.012449399     -0.030600358      0.004191544




def lm_morantest(y, X, B):
    """Moran's I test for the residuals of a linear model (Cliff & Ord), two-sided"""
    W = B / B.sum(1, keepdims=True); U = 0.5 * (W + W.T); N, p = X.shape
    S0 = U.sum(); S1 = 0.5 * ((2 * U) ** 2).sum()
    XtXinv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    u = y - X @ XtXinv @ X.T @ y  # residuals
    I = N / S0 * (u @ U @ u) / (u @ u)
    Z_ = U @ X; C1 = X.T @ Z_; C3 = XtXinv @ C1
    trA = np.trace(C3); EI = -(N * trA) / ((N - p) * S0)
    trA2 = np.trace(C3 @ C3); trB = np.trace(4 * XtXinv @ (Z_.T @ Z_))
    VI = (N * N / (S0 * S0 * (N - p) * (N - p + 2))) * (S1 + 2 * trA2 - trB - 2 * trA ** 2 / (N - p))
    Z = (I - EI) / np.sqrt(VI)
    return pd.Series(dict(I=I, expectation=EI, variance=VI, z=Z, p_value=2 * norm.sf(abs(Z))))

X_trend = np.column_stack([np.ones(64), Var1])  # x_t ~ Var1
lm_morantest(x_t, X_trend, B_queen)
# I             -0.012449
# expectation   -0.030600
# variance       0.004192
# z              0.280358
# p_value        0.779203
# dtype: float64




This is important to understand because the spatial patterning in a variable of interest, and picked up by a global measure of spatial autocorrelation, may be driven by an omitted variable. If we cannot add that variable, a latent variable or mixed effects model may be a good choice.

title: 15  Measures of spatial autocorrelation
text:
Exercise 15.3
False discovery rate adjustment is required when conducting repeated tests on the same data set. Usually, local measures of spatial autocorrelation are calculated for all the observations in a data set, and so constitute repeated tests. When repeated tests are conducted, the usual reading of confidence intervals and probability values must be adjusted to take the repeated use of the data into account.

title: 15  Measures of spatial autocorrelation
text:
Exercise 15.4
If we start with the standard local Moran’s \(I_i\) for the random values with a slight 1D trend, upgraded to analytical conditional standard deviates, but with only the standard intercept-only mean model, we have a starting point; a fair number of the values exceed 2:


R
Python




locm <- localmoran(x_t, nb2listw(queen, style="W"))




def local_moran(x, B):
    """local Moran's I, with analytical conditional moments, two-sided"""
    W = B / B.sum(1, keepdims=True); n = len(x); z = x - x.mean(); lz = W @ z
    s2 = (z ** 2).sum() / n; Ii = z / s2 * lz
    Wi, Wi2, m2 = W.sum(1), (W ** 2).sum(1), (z * z).sum() / n
    E = -(z ** 2 * Wi) / ((n - 1) * m2)
    V = (z / m2) ** 2 * (n / (n - 2)) * (Wi2 - Wi ** 2 / (n - 1)) * (m2 - z ** 2 / (n - 1))
    Z = (Ii - E) / np.sqrt(V)
    return pd.DataFrame(dict(Ii=Ii, E_Ii=E, Var_Ii=V, Z_Ii=Z, p_value=2 * norm.sf(abs(Z))))

locm = local_moran(x_t, B_queen)






R
Python




plot(density(locm[, 4]))
abline(v=c(-2, 2))










def density_plot(v):
    g = np.linspace(v.min() - 1, v.max() + 1, 200)
    plt.plot(g, gaussian_kde(v)(g))
    plt.axvline(-2, color="black"); plt.axvline(2, color="black")
    plt.show()

density_plot(locm.Z_Ii.to_numpy())












R
Python




grd$locm_sd <- locm[, 4]
plot(grd[, "locm_sd"]) 










def map_plot(values, name):
    grd.assign(**{name: values}).plot(column=name, legend=True)
    plt.axis("off"); plt.title(name); plt.show()

map_plot(locm.Z_Ii.to_numpy(), "locm_sd")












R
Python




sum(p.adjust(locm[, 5], method="none") < 0.05)
# [1] 6




(locm.p_value < 0.05).sum()  # p.adjust(method = "none")
# np.int64(6)




If we apply false discovery rate adjustment, we have just one significant measure:


R
Python




sum(p.adjust(locm[, 5], method="fdr") < 0.05)
# [1] 1




multipletests(locm.p_value, method="fdr_bh")[0].sum()  # p.adjust(method = "fdr")
# np.int64(1)




In the first Saddlepoint approximation also for the random values with a slight 1D trend, the distribution of standard deviates shifts leftward, with both positive and negative values beyond abs(2):


R
Python




lm_null <- lm(x_t ~ 1)
locm_null <- summary(localmoran.sad(lm_null, nb=queen, style="W"))




def local_moran_sad(y, X, B):
    """saddlepoint approximation for local Moran's I (row-standardized "W" style),
    for the residuals of the linear model y ~ X; two-sided"""
    n, p = X.shape; m = n - p - 2
    XtXinv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    u = y - X @ XtXinv @ X.T @ y; utu = u @ u
    D = 1 / B.sum(1); out = []
    for i in range(n):
        Vi = np.zeros((n, n)); w = n * D[i] * B[i] / 2  # symmetric "star" matrix for region i
        Vi[i, :] = w; Vi[:, i] = w
        Ii = u @ Vi @ u / utu
        ViX = Vi @ X; MViM = X.T @ ViX @ XtXinv
        t1 = -np.trace(MViM)
        t2 = (Vi ** 2).sum() - 2 * np.trace(ViX.T @ ViX @ XtXinv) + np.trace(MViM @ MViM)
        e1 = 0.5 * (t1 + np.sqrt(2 * t2 - t1 ** 2)); en = 0.5 * (t1 - np.sqrt(2 * t2 - t1 ** 2))
        l, h, mi = en, e1, Ii
        a_ = m * mi * (l + h - 2 * mi) + mi * (3 * l + 3 * h - 4 * mi) - 2 * l * h
        b_ = (m + 2) * mi * (l - mi) * (h - mi)
        c1 = l ** 2 * mi ** 2 * (m + 1) ** 2 + h ** 2 * mi ** 2 * (m + 1) ** 2
        c2 = 2 * l * h * (2 * l * h - 2 * l * mi - 2 * h * mi - 2 * m * mi ** 2 - m ** 2 * mi ** 2 + mi ** 2)
        om = 0.25 * (a_ - np.sqrt(c1 + c2)) / b_
        taumi = np.concatenate([[e1], np.zeros(m), [en]]) - Ii
        r = np.sign(om) * np.sqrt(np.log(1 - 2 * om * taumi).sum())
        uu = om * np.sqrt(2 * (taumi ** 2 / (1 - 2 * om * taumi) ** 2).sum())
        sad = r - np.log(r / uu) / r
        out.append((Ii, sad, 2 * norm.sf(abs(sad))))
    return pd.DataFrame(out, columns=["Ii", "Saddlepoint", "Pr_Sad"])

locm_null = local_moran_sad(x_t, np.ones((64, 1)), B_queen)  # x_t ~ 1

Python

abline(v=c(-2, 2))

# [1] 8




(locm_null.Pr_Sad < 0.05).sum()
# np.int64(8)




If we apply false discovery rate adjustment, we also have just one significant measure:

Python

# [1] 1




multipletests(locm_null.Pr_Sad, method="fdr_bh")[0].sum()
# np.int64(1)




Once we analyse a model including the 1D trend, most of the distribution of standard deviate values is between -2 and 2:


R
Python




lm_trend <- lm(x_t ~ xy$Var1)
locm_tr <- summary(localmoran.sad(lm_trend, nb=queen, style="W"))




locm_tr = local_moran_sad(x_t, X_trend, B_queen)  # x_t ~ Var1






R
Python

abline(v=c(-2, 2))










density_plot(locm_tr.Saddlepoint.to_numpy())












R
Python

plot(grd[, "locm_tr_sd"]) 










map_plot(locm_tr.Saddlepoint.to_numpy(), "locm_tr_sd")












R
Python




sum(p.adjust(locm_tr[, "Pr. (Sad)"], method="none") < 0.05)
# [1] 2




(locm_tr.Pr_Sad < 0.05).sum()
# np.int64(2)




If we apply false discovery rate adjustment, we now have no significant measures, as expected:


R
Python




sum(p.adjust(locm_tr[, "Pr. (Sad)"], method="fdr") < 0.05)
# [1] 0




multipletests(locm_tr.Pr_Sad, method="fdr_bh")[0].sum()
# np.int64(0)




localmoran.sad() or localmoran.exact() provide both richer mean models, and estimates of the standard deviates built on the underlying spatial relationships for each observation, rather than analytical or permutation assumptions for the whole data set. This is achieved at the cost of longer compute times and larger memory use, especially when the Omega= argument to localmoran.sad() or localmoran.exact.alt() is used, because this is a dense \(n \times n\) matrix.

# 
#   Moran I test under randomisation
# 
# data:  depmunic$prgreensp  
# weights: spdep::nb2listw(mun_nb)    
# 
# Moran I statistic standard deviate = 1.825, p-value = 0.034
# alternative hypothesis: greater
# sample estimates:
# Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
#        0.22384238       -0.16666667        0.04578844




def moran_test(x, g):
    """Moran's I test under randomisation, row-standardised weights, one-sided
    (alternative "greater"), like spdep::moran.test()"""
    m = esda.Moran(np.asarray(x), g.transform("r").to_W(), permutations=0)
    return pd.Series(dict(I=m.I, expectation=m.EI, variance=m.VI_rand,
                          z=m.z_rand, p_value=norm.sf(m.z_rand)))

# k = 4 nearest neighbours, made symmetric. There are only 575 distinct locations
# for the 1000 properties, and libpysal's Graph.build_knn() refuses coincident points
# (as does the kd-tree in spdep, which falls back to brute force); here ties between
# identical locations are broken by row order, as the brute-force search in spdep does
xy = np.column_stack([properties.geometry.x, properties.geometry.y])
D = cdist(xy, xy)
np.fill_diagonal(D, np.inf)
nn = np.argsort(D, axis=1, kind="stable")[:, :4]
A = sparse.csr_matrix((np.ones(nn.size), (np.repeat(np.arange(len(xy)), 4), nn.ravel())),
                      shape=(len(xy), len(xy)))
pr_nb_k4s = graph.Graph.from_sparse(((A + A.T) > 0).astype(float), ids=properties["id"].to_numpy())
nb_summary(pr_nb_k4s)
# Number of regions: 1000
# Number of nonzero links: 5874
# Average number of links: 5.874
# Disjoint connected subgraphs: 5




Copying out has led to the introduction of very powerful positive spatial autocorrelation in this and other variables copied out:

Exercise 16.3
The vignette proposes the full property level and municipal department level set of variables straight away. Here we choose the property level ones first, and update for the copied out municipal department level ones next:


R
Python




f_pr <- prpsqm ~ size + age + dist_metro
f_pr_md <- update(f_pr, . ~ . + foreigners + prgreensp + popdens + museums + airbnb)

f_pr_md = f_pr + " + foreigners + prgreensp + popdens + museums + airbnb"




Adding in the copied out upper level variables appears to account for more of the variability of the response than leaving them out:


R
Python




library(mgcv)
# Loading required package: nlme
# This is mgcv 1.9-4. For overview type '?mgcv'.
pr_base <- gam(f_pr, data=properties_in_dd)
pr_2lev <- gam(f_pr_md, data=properties_in_dd)
anova(pr_base, pr_2lev, test="Chisq")
# Analysis of Deviance Table
# 
# Model 1: prpsqm ~ size + age + dist_metro
# Model 2: prpsqm ~ size + age + dist_metro + foreigners + prgreensp + popdens + 
#     museums + airbnb
#   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df  Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
# 1       996  625149227                           
# 2       991  524571512  5 100577716 < 2.2e-16 ***
# ---
# Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




# mgcv::gam() with only parametric terms is a linear model
pr_base = smf.ols(f_pr, properties_in_dd).fit()
pr_2lev = smf.ols(f_pr_md, properties_in_dd).fit()

def anova_chisq(small, big):
    """analysis of deviance table with a chi-square test, scale from the larger model,
    like anova(small, big, test = "Chisq") on gam objects"""
    ddf = small.df_resid - big.df_resid
    dev = small.ssr - big.ssr
    scale = big.ssr / big.df_resid
    return pd.DataFrame({"Resid. Df": [small.df_resid, big.df_resid],
                         "Resid. Dev": [small.ssr, big.ssr],
                         "Df": [np.nan, ddf], "Deviance": [np.nan, dev],
                         "Pr(>Chi)": [np.nan, chi2.sf(dev / scale, ddf)]})

anova_chisq(pr_base, pr_2lev)

Adding an upper level IID random effect to the base formula also improves the fit of the model substantially:


R
Python




pr_base_iid <- gam(update(f_pr, . ~ . + s(num_dep, bs="re")), data=properties_in_dd)
anova(pr_base, pr_base_iid, test="Chisq")
# Analysis of Deviance Table
# 
# Model 1: prpsqm ~ size + age + dist_metro
# Model 2: prpsqm ~ size + age + dist_metro + s(num_dep, bs = "re")
#   Resid. Df Resid. Dev      Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
# 1       996  625149227                               
# 2       995  557913777 0.99993 67235450 < 2.2e-16 ***
# ---
# Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




# IID random effect for the municipality department: a random intercept, fitted with
# statsmodels' MixedLM (the lme4 analogue; REML for the estimates, ML for the
# likelihood ratio tests, as REML likelihoods are not comparable across fixed effects).
# Note that the R chunk uses the integer num_dep in s(num_dep, bs = "re"), which gives a
# random slope; the factor conversion only happens in exercise 16.4. With a factor, gam
# (method = "REML"), lme4 and MixedLM all give the same estimates.
def fit_iid(formula, reml):
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        return smf.mixedlm(formula, properties_in_dd,
                           groups=properties_in_dd["num_dep"]).fit(reml=reml)

def lrt_iid(fixed_only, formula):
    """likelihood ratio test of the random intercept (variance on the boundary of the
    parameter space, so the chi-square(1) p-value is halved)"""
    ols_ml, iid_ml = fixed_only, fit_iid(formula, reml=False)
    stat = 2 * (iid_ml.llf - ols_ml.llf)
    return pd.Series({"logLik (fixed only)": ols_ml.llf, "logLik (with IID)": iid_ml.llf,
                      "LR statistic": stat, "p-value": 0.5 * chi2.sf(stat, 1)})

pr_base_iid = fit_iid(f_pr, reml=True)
lrt_iid(pr_base, f_pr)

The "mrf" smooth term needs ID keys set so that the neighbour object is correctly matched to the observations. Once these are provided, the properties level model with a municipality department level MRF smooth may be fit:

text:
Exercise 17.1
First create a spatial weights object from the k=4 symmetrized neighbour object:
Fit a linear model to the lower-level data; all the included variables seem worth retaining:
However, there is strong residual autocorrelation:
Robust (adjusted) Lagrange multiplier tests (Rao’s score tests) suggest that the fitted model should include a spatial autoregressive process in the residuals, but not in the response:
Adding in the copied out municipality department level variables, we see that they do not seem to be worth retaining (unless there are good reasons for doing so); they do however improve model fit:
The pre-test results are similar to those for the properties-only variables:
and the LM tests continue to indicate an omitted spatial process in the residual rather than the response:

library(spdep)
lm.morantest(LM_pr, lw)
# 
#   Global Moran I for regression residuals
# 
# data:  
# model: lm(formula = f_pr, data = properties_in_dd)
# weights: lw
# 
# Moran I statistic standard deviate = 26.039, p-value <
# 2.2e-16
# alternative hypothesis: greater
# sample estimates:
# Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
#     0.4872794374    -0.0023026155     0.0003535235




def lm_morantest(model, B=Bk):
    """Moran's I test for linear model residuals (Cliff & Ord), one-sided
    (alternative "greater"), like spdep::lm.morantest(); B: binary neighbours"""
    y_, X = model.model.endog, model.model.exog
    Wr = B / B.sum(1, keepdims=True); U = 0.5 * (Wr + Wr.T); N, p = X.shape
    S0 = U.sum(); S1 = 0.5 * ((2 * U) ** 2).sum(); XtXinv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    u = y_ - X @ XtXinv @ X.T @ y_
    I = N / S0 * (u @ U @ u) / (u @ u)
    Z_ = U @ X; C3 = XtXinv @ (X.T @ Z_); trA = np.trace(C3)
    EI = -(N * trA) / ((N - p) * S0)
    VI = (N * N / (S0 * S0 * (N - p) * (N - p + 2))) * (
        S1 + 2 * np.trace(C3 @ C3) - np.trace(4 * XtXinv @ (Z_.T @ Z_)) - 2 * trA ** 2 / (N - p))
    z = (I - EI) / np.sqrt(VI)
    return pd.Series(dict(I=I, expectation=EI, variance=VI, z=z, p_value=norm.sf(z)))

# test weights: lw

# adjRSlag = 1.2688, df = 1, p-value = 0.26




def rs_tests(model, w=lw):
    """adjusted Rao score tests for spatial error and lag dependence (the robust LM tests
    of Anselin et al.), via spreg's spatial diagnostics for OLS"""
    o = spreg.OLS(model.model.endog.reshape(-1, 1), model.model.exog[:, 1:],  # spreg adds the constant
                  w=w, spat_diag=True)
    return pd.DataFrame({"statistic": [o.rlm_error[0], o.rlm_lag[0]],
                         "p_value": [o.rlm_error[1], o.rlm_lag[1]]}, index=["adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"])

# Hausman test: -246.29, df: 4, p-value: < 2.22e-16




def hausman_test(y_, X, W, lam, s2):
    """spatial Hausman test of OLS against the spatial error model, as spatialreg::Hausman.test().
    Vo follows spatialreg's Hcov, which uses A A with A = (I - lambda W)^-1 (not A A'),
    for which the statistic need not be positive"""
    y_ = np.asarray(y_).ravel(); B = np.eye(len(y_)) - lam * W; A = np.linalg.inv(B)
    R = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X); Xs, ys = B @ X, B @ y_
    d = R @ X.T @ y_ - np.linalg.solve(Xs.T @ Xs, Xs.T @ ys)    # OLS minus SEM coefficients
    Vo = s2 * (R @ X.T @ A @ A @ X @ R); Vs = s2 * np.linalg.inv(Xs.T @ Xs)
    stat = float(d @ np.linalg.solve(Vo - Vs, d))
    return pd.Series(dict(statistic=stat, df=len(d), p_value=chi2.sf(abs(stat), len(d))))

def impacts_slx(coef, cov, names, kx):
    """direct (own), indirect (lagged X) and total impacts of SLX and SDEM models, with standard
    errors from the coefficient covariance (the "glht" impacts of spatialreg)"""
    rows = []
    for j, nm in enumerate(names):
        i_b, i_t = 1 + j, 1 + kx + j
        b, t = coef[i_b], coef[i_t]
        v_b, v_t, c = cov[i_b, i_b], cov[i_t, i_t], cov[i_b, i_t]
        rows.append(dict(variable=nm, direct=b, indirect=t, total=b + t,
                         se_direct=v_b ** .5, se_indirect=v_t ** .5, se_total=(v_b + v_t + 2 * c) ** .5))
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable")
    for c in ["direct", "indirect", "total"]:
        out["z_" + c] = out[c] / out["se_" + c]
        out["p_" + c] = 2 * norm.sf(abs(out["z_" + c]))
    return out

title: 17  Spatial econometrics models
text:
Exercise 17.4
Turning to estimating the general nested model first, followed by excluding the Durbin (spatially lagged \(X\)) variables, a likelihood ratio test shows that the spatially lagged \(X\) variables should be retained in the model:


R
Python




GNM_pr <- sacsarlm(f_pr, data=properties_in_dd, listw=lw, Durbin=TRUE,
    control=list(pre_eig1=eigs, pre_eig2=eigs))




# spreg has ML estimation of spatial error, lag and Durbin models, but not of the SAC and
# general nested models (GNM). This is a compact implementation of ML estimation by maximising the
# concentrated log-likelihood over rho and lambda, with the log-determinants from the
# eigenvalues of W (pre_eig in R); standard errors come from the numerical Hessian of
# the full log-likelihood, so they differ somewhat from the analytical ones of spatialreg
def logdet(r, ev):  # ln|I - r W|
    return np.log(np.abs(1 - r * ev)).sum()

def sac_loglik(theta, y_, X, W, ev, rho, lam):
    k = X.shape[1]; b = theta[:k]
    r = theta[k] if rho else 0.0; l = theta[k + 1] if lam else 0.0; s2 = theta[k + 2]
    res = (y_ - r * (W @ y_)) - X @ b
    e = res - l * (W @ res)
    return -len(y_) / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s2) - e @ e / (2 * s2) + logdet(r, ev) + logdet(l, ev)

def sac_concentrated(r, l, y_, X, W, ev):  # ML estimates of beta and sigma^2 given rho, lambda
    ys = (y_ - r * (W @ y_)) - l * (W @ (y_ - r * (W @ y_)))
    Xs = X - l * (W @ X)
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(Xs, ys, rcond=None)[0]
    s2 = ((ys - Xs @ b) ** 2).mean()
    return b, s2

def num_hessian(f, x0, h=1e-4):
    k = len(x0); H = np.zeros((k, k)); st = h * np.maximum(1.0, np.abs(x0))
    for i in range(k):
        for j in range(i, k):
            ei = np.zeros(k); ej = np.zeros(k); ei[i] = st[i]; ej[j] = st[j]
            H[i, j] = H[j, i] = (f(x0 + ei + ej) - f(x0 + ei - ej) - f(x0 - ei + ej) + f(x0 - ei - ej)) / (4 * st[i] * st[j])
    return H

def _put(theta, idx, t):
    out = theta.copy(); out[idx] = t
    return out

def fit_sac(variables, durbin, rho=True, lam=True):
    """SAC (durbin = []) or GNM (durbin = names of the variables with lagged X)"""
    Xv = properties_in_dd[variables].to_numpy()
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Xv] + ([Wd @ properties_in_dd[durbin].to_numpy()] if durbin else []))
    y_ = y.ravel(); lo = 1 / eigs.real.min()
    def nll(p):
        r, l = (p[0] if rho else 0.0), (p[1] if lam else 0.0)
        b, s2 = sac_concentrated(r, l, y_, X, Wd, eigs)
        return -sac_loglik(np.concatenate([b, [r, l, s2]]), y_, X, Wd, eigs, rho, lam)
    best = None
    for start in [(0.5, 0.5), (0.8, -0.8), (-0.3, 0.3), (0.0, 0.0)]:
        res = so.minimize(nll, start, method="L-BFGS-B", bounds=[(lo + 1e-3, 0.999)] * 2)
        if best is None or res.fun < best.fun:
            best = res
    r, l = (best.x[0] if rho else 0.0), (best.x[1] if lam else 0.0)
    b, s2 = sac_concentrated(r, l, y_, X, Wd, eigs)
    theta = np.concatenate([b, [r, l, s2]])
    free = np.array([True] * X.shape[1] + [rho, lam, True])
    idx = np.flatnonzero(free)
    H = num_hessian(lambda t: sac_loglik(_put(theta, idx, t), y_, X, Wd, eigs, rho, lam), theta[idx])
    cov = np.linalg.inv(-H)
    names = ["(Intercept)"] + variables + ["lag." + d for d in durbin]
    return dict(theta=theta, free=free, cov=cov, idx=idx, names=names, variables=variables, durbin=durbin,
                rho=r, lam=l, s2=s2, loglik=sac_loglik(theta, y_, X, Wd, eigs, rho, lam), df=int(free.sum()),
                se=np.sqrt(np.diag(cov)))

def sac_table(fit):
    k = len(fit["names"])
    tab = pd.DataFrame({"Estimate": fit["theta"][:k], "Std. Error": fit["se"][:k]}, index=fit["names"])
    tab["z value"] = tab["Estimate"] / tab["Std. Error"]
    print(f"rho: {fit['rho']:.4f} (se {fit['se'][k]:.4f}), lambda: {fit['lam']:.4f} (se {fit['se'][k + 1]:.4f})")
    print(f"log likelihood: {fit['loglik']:.3f}, df: {fit['df']}")
    return tab

GNM_pr = fit_sac(xn, xn)
sac_table(GNM_pr)
# rho: 0.8801 (se 0.0133), lambda: -0.8970 (se 0.0539)
# log likelihood: -7783.902, df: 10
#                  Estimate  Std. Error    z value
# (Intercept)     80.501054   40.086163   2.008201
# size             2.729839    0.355858   7.671151
# age            -23.886207    1.023088 -23.347156
# dist_metro       0.337037    0.235918   1.428616
# lag.size        -1.184819    0.553547  -2.140413
# lag.age         23.161294    1.320910  17.534346
# lag.dist_metro  -0.381096    0.241040  -1.581047






R
Python




SARAR_pr <- sacsarlm(f_pr, data=properties_in_dd, listw=lw, 
    control=list(pre_eig1=eigs, pre_eig2=eigs))

def lrtest(m0, m1):
    """likelihood ratio test of two nested models (each a dict with loglik and df)"""
    stat = 2 * (m1["loglik"] - m0["loglik"]); df = m1["df"] - m0["df"]
    return pd.DataFrame({"#Df": [m0["df"], m1["df"]], "LogLik": [m0["loglik"], m1["loglik"]],
                         "Df": [np.nan, df], "Chisq": [np.nan, stat],
                         "Pr(>Chisq)": [np.nan, chi2.sf(stat, df)]}, index=["model 1", "model 2"])

def impacts_sac(fit, R=2000, seed=4807):
    """direct, indirect and total impacts of a GNM, with simulation based standard errors;
    the traces of the powers of W follow from the eigenvalues, so no trW() is needed"""
    names, durbin = fit["variables"], fit["durbin"]; kx = len(fit["names"])
    k = len(names); sel = list(range(kx)) + [kx]            # coefficients and rho
    mean, cov = fit["theta"][sel], fit["cov"][np.ix_(sel, sel)]
    def one(p):
        b, r = p[:kx], p[kx]
        trS = (1 / (1 - r * eigs)).real.sum(); trSW = (eigs / (1 - r * eigs)).real.sum()
        out = []
        for j, nm in enumerate(names):
            bb = b[1 + j]; tt = b[1 + k + durbin.index(nm)] if nm in durbin else 0.0
            d = (bb * trS + tt * trSW) / n; tot = (bb + tt) / (1 - r)
            out.append((d, tot - d, tot))
        return np.array(out)
    est = one(mean)
    sims = np.array([one(p) for p in np.random.default_rng(seed).multivariate_normal(mean, cov, R)])
    se = sims.std(axis=0, ddof=1); z = est / se; cols = ["direct", "indirect", "total"]
    return pd.concat({"impact": pd.DataFrame(est, index=names, columns=cols),
                      "se": pd.DataFrame(se, index=names, columns=cols),
                      "z": pd.DataFrame(z, index=names, columns=cols),
                      "p": pd.DataFrame(2 * norm.sf(abs(z)), index=names, columns=cols)}, axis=1)

title: 17  Spatial econometrics models
text:
Exercise 17.5
We cannot say that the spatial econometrics approach has reached a clear conclusion. When including the upper level variables, we introduce a lot of spatial autocorrelation at the lower level. It is arguable that the MRF random effect at the upper level and including only the properties level variables gets at least as far as the most complex spatial econometrics models. It is fairly clear that mapping the actual green space and museums, and measuring distance from each property to the attractions would remove the scale problem for those variables. Disaggregation of the foreigners, airbnb and population density variables would be highly desirable. With improvements to the properties level data set, including more variables describing the properties themselves, much of the mis-specification should be removed.
